title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator‑detectable failures were absent on this curated task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the preregistered design, the deterministic accounting that established single shared generations per task, the Mininet 10% holdout concordance check (no disagreements observed), a prominent disclosure of a missing labeled selection seed for that holdout, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs, operational implications, and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains but raises safety risks when generated changes are incorrect or violate workflow constraints, potentially causing outages or policy breaches. Prior work therefore proposes grounding and verifier‑assisted repair loops—commonly framed as generate–validate–repair (GVR) or RAG+repair architectures—to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the operational benefit of automated repair depends on the prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generation policy and on validator fidelity. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question to measure the marginal effect of deterministic GVR on validator‑detected failures: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study used a paired shared‑initial design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the effect of invoking the validator and (if needed) a single automated repair call on that identical output. Contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered paired measurement on 200 machine‑checkable NetOps tasks with deterministic accounting; (2) an empirical null result with full execution accounting (no validator failures observed under the chosen generator/prompt policy); and (3) an artifact‑grounded analysis of methodological tradeoffs, validator coverage limits, and reproducibility gaps that inform future confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies document frequent LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism across domains, and propose grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and conservative guardrail architectures as mitigations. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but typically lack instrumented, externally auditable failure‑rate studies. Architectural proposals and small‑scale systems integrate deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checks or similar) with LLM generation to reduce unsafe outputs; red‑team and audit work shows agentic tool descriptions and chaining can change safety outcomes and create configuration‑level brittleness. Collectively, prior work motivates controlled, preregistered measurements that isolate when validator‑assisted repair reduces validator‑detectable errors and where validator blind spots limit safety claims.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and inferential plan. The sealed preregistration (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) specified a paired design with n = 200 tasks, a single deterministic shared initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrapped paired‑difference percentile 95% confidence intervals were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline validator failure prevalence ≈30% and a targeted 50% relative reduction; these assumptions informed sample size but remain separate from observed data.
sections.results: Execution and accounting. The run completed all planned episodes and pairs. Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0. The primary deterministic validator reported baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0]. No repair branch was invoked because initial candidates passed the validator in every case. Secondary analyses preplanned for repaired cases (repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, model‑call cost per repair) are empty because no repairs occurred.
sections.discussion: Conditional interpretation. The observed null is an artifact‑grounded result: under the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), prompts, and the adapter's shared‑initial deterministic invocation semantics, validator‑detectable failures were absent for the curated task bank. This outcome does not prove that GVR is unnecessary in general; rather, it demonstrates that the marginal utility of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and on validator coverage for the evaluated workload. Diagnostics explaining the null include archived validator traces showing that generator outputs satisfied the tasks' machine‑checkable required_sequence and constraint checks and difficulty labels ("medium"/"hard"/"very_hard") indicating nontrivial workflow patterns were exercised despite correct outputs.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study (n = 200) comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All initial candidates passed the primary validator (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The results emphasize that (a) GVR's operational benefit is workload dependent; (b) practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence and validator fidelity before allocating repair budgets; and (c) future confirmatory runs should consider mixed designs that include independent multi‑sample draws, larger emulation holdouts with recorded selection seeds, richer validator models, and larger or multi‑step repair budgets to characterize practical gains.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
